subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Classifying and grouping countries by development
The development gap and its causes

questions.q: What does the economic development indicator GNI stand for?
options: Gross National Income
Gross National Industry
Global Natural Income
Gross National Investment
questions.explain: GNI (Gross National Income) is the total income earned by a country's people and businesses, usually shown per capita.

questions.q: The infant mortality rate measures the number of deaths of children under one year old per:
options: 1,000 live births per year
100 people per year
1,000 women of childbearing age
10,000 adults per year
questions.explain: Infant mortality is measured as deaths of babies under one year per 1,000 live births, and it falls as development rises.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) is expressed as a value between:
options: 0 and 1
0 and 10
1 and 100
-1 and +1
questions.explain: HDI ranges from 0 to 1, with values closer to 1 showing higher levels of development.

questions.q: The literacy rate is best defined as:
options: the percentage of adults who can read and write
the percentage of children who attend school
the average number of years spent in education
the number of universities per million people
questions.explain: The literacy rate is a social indicator showing the proportion of adults able to read and write.

questions.q: In development studies, what does the abbreviation NIC stand for?
options: Newly Industrialised Country
National Investment Company
Northern Industrial Continent
New International Currency
questions.explain: NICs, such as China and India, are countries whose economies have industrialised rapidly in recent decades.

questions.q: The Brandt Line is an imaginary line that divides the world into:
options: a wealthier 'North' and a poorer 'South'
an industrial 'East' and a rural 'West'
developed islands and developing mainlands
high-birth-rate and low-birth-rate nations
questions.explain: The Brandt Line separates richer, more developed countries of the global North from poorer countries of the global South.

questions.q: The term 'development gap' refers to:
options: the difference in wealth and wellbeing between the richest and poorest countries
the time it takes a country to industrialise
the gap between a country's birth rate and death rate
the distance between a country and the Equator
questions.explain: The development gap is the difference in standards of living between the world's richest and poorest countries.

questions.q: A key feature of Fairtrade is that it:
options: guarantees producers a fair, minimum price for their goods
removes all taxes on exported goods
gives farmers free land from the government
bans trade between rich and poor countries
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees producers a minimum price plus a premium to invest in their communities.

questions.q: Why can GNI per capita be misleading as a measure of development when used on its own?
options: It is an average that can hide large inequalities in how wealth is shared
It only counts income earned by women
It cannot be measured in US dollars
It ignores the total population of the country
questions.explain: As a mean figure, GNI per capita can mask great inequalities between rich and poor within a country.

questions.q: The HDI is a composite indicator that combines income with which two other measures?
options: life expectancy and education
birth rate and death rate
employment and housing quality
energy use and internet access
questions.explain: HDI combines GNI per capita with life expectancy and education to give a broader picture of development.

questions.q: Incomes are often converted to 'purchasing power parity' (PPP) so that:
options: differences in the cost of living between countries are taken into account
only the richest households are included
figures can be shown in each local currency
inflation is completely removed from all data
questions.explain: PPP adjusts income figures for the local cost of living, making comparisons between countries fairer.

questions.q: The World Bank commonly groups countries by income into low-income, middle-income and:
options: high-income countries
no-income countries
coastal-income countries
colonial-income countries
questions.explain: The World Bank classifies economies as low-, middle- or high-income based mainly on GNI per capita.

questions.q: Why does dependence on exporting primary products (raw materials) often slow a country's development?
options: their prices are often low and can change sharply on world markets
they can only be sold to neighbouring countries
they are always banned by richer nations
they use up all of a country's manufactured goods
questions.explain: Primary products usually earn low, unstable prices, so relying on them limits and destabilises income.

questions.q: How did colonialism contribute to the development gap for many countries?
options: colonial powers extracted raw materials and left economies dependent and undiversified
colonial powers built equal industries in every colony
colonies were given complete control of world trade
colonial rule removed all of a country's national debt
questions.explain: Colonial powers exploited colonies for raw materials, leaving many with narrow, dependent economies after independence.

questions.q: Which physical factor can hold back a country's development?
options: being landlocked, making trade more difficult and costly
having a coastline with natural harbours
having a stable, temperate climate
having a large, well-educated workforce
questions.explain: Landlocked countries face higher transport costs and reduced access to sea trade, which can hinder development.

questions.q: Appropriate (intermediate) technology is best described as technology that:
options: suits the skills, resources and needs of local people
is always the most advanced available anywhere
can only be operated by foreign engineers
requires large amounts of imported fuel
questions.explain: Appropriate technology, such as simple hand pumps, matches local skills and resources so communities can maintain it themselves.

questions.q: Country X has an infant mortality rate of 4 and life expectancy of 82; Country Y has an infant mortality rate of 60 and life expectancy of 54. What can you conclude?
options: Country X is more developed than Country Y
Country Y is more developed than Country X
The two countries are at the same level of development
No conclusion can be drawn from these indicators
questions.explain: Low infant mortality and high life expectancy point to better welfare, so Country X is more developed.

questions.q: A country has a fairly high GNI per capita, yet low life expectancy and low literacy. This most likely suggests that:
options: the country's wealth is not being shared or spent to improve people's welfare
the country has no natural resources at all
GNI per capita must have been measured incorrectly
the country must have a very small population
questions.explain: A mismatch between high income and poor social indicators suggests wealth is unevenly shared or not invested in welfare.

questions.q: An NGO installs simple hand pumps that villagers can repair themselves using local materials. Which strategy to reduce the development gap does this best illustrate?
options: appropriate technology
debt relief
free trade agreements
large-scale industrialisation
questions.explain: Hand pumps maintained by local people using local resources are a classic example of appropriate technology.

questions.q: A low-income country has much of its international debt cancelled. What is the most likely benefit?
options: the government can spend more money on services such as health and education
the country must immediately repay all remaining loans
the country is banned from all future trade
the country's population automatically decreases
questions.explain: Debt relief frees up government money that can be redirected into development priorities such as healthcare and schooling.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Development & Human Welfare
